The most familiar example is the apartment building entry system. A visitor at the locked front door presses your unit's button, you hear them speak from a wall unit inside your apartment, and you can buzz the door open — all without going downstairs.

In offices and workplaces:
Office intercom systems let a manager speak directly to a specific employee's desk, or make an announcement to an entire floor. This is far quicker than walking across the building or sending a message.

In hospitals:
Nurses use intercom systems to communicate with patients in their rooms, or to call for help quickly. A patient pressing the call button beside their bed is essentially triggering a one-way intercom to the nurses' station.

In aircraft:
Pilots and crew members use an intercom system — sometimes called a "flight intercom" — to talk to each other inside the aircraft, separate from the radio they use to communicate with air traffic control. Passengers using a call button to speak with a flight attendant also interact with a version of this system.

In ships:
Large naval or commercial ships use intercoms to allow the captain on the bridge to communicate instantly with the engine room, the deck crew, or other sections of the vessel.

In homes:
Some homes have a built-in intercom system that connects rooms — for example, the front door to the kitchen, or a parent's room to a baby's room. A baby monitor is essentially a simple, one-way home intercom: it picks up sound in the baby's room and transmits it to a receiver the parent carries.

In restaurants:
Drive-through fast food systems use a form of intercom — you speak into a post with a microphone outside, and a staff member inside hears you and responds through a speaker next to you.

In security systems:
Intercoms are widely used as part of security setups, where a guard post or reception desk can screen visitors before granting them access.

A modern development worth knowing: many intercoms today also include a camera and a screen. These are called video intercoms (or video door phones). Instead of just hearing the person at your door, you can also see them on a small screen. This adds an important layer of security — you can visually confirm who is there before allowing them in. Smart doorbells (like the popular ones from companies like Ring or Nest) are consumer-grade video intercoms.

Traditional intercoms use physical wires running through walls and ceilings to connect all the units together. These are reliable and common in older buildings.

Modern intercoms are often wireless, using radio signals or Wi-Fi to connect units. These are easier to install and more flexible — you can even link them to your smartphone.

To solidify your understanding, here is how the word is used naturally in sentences:

  • "The delivery person rang the intercom, and I buzzed him in from my apartment."
  • "The pilot's voice came through the intercom, announcing a slight delay."
  • "The school installed a new intercom system so the principal could address all classrooms simultaneously."
  • "She heard her baby stir through the intercom on her bedside table."
  • "The security guard at the gate spoke to visitors through an intercom before opening the barrier."

An intercom is a closed, self-contained communication system that allows people in different but nearby locations to speak to each other — or to broadcast a message to others — without a telephone network, without physical proximity, and without delay. It is built for a specific environment and only connects the specific stations or units within that environment. It can be two-way (a conversation) or one-way (an announcement), it can carry voice alone or voice and video, and it can be wired or wireless. You encounter intercoms in apartment buildings, offices, hospitals, aircraft, ships, homes, and security setups — anywhere there is a need for quick, reliable, private communication between fixed points.
8942:
Intercourse means a meaningful exchange or interaction between two or more parties. Think of it as two sides actively engaging with each other — not just existing near one another, but genuinely connecting and exchanging something. That "something" could be words, ideas, goods, feelings, or physical intimacy, depending on the context.

The word has two distinct senses: a broad, general one and a specific, physical one. Both are completely standard and found in reputable dictionaries.
Sense 1 — General: Communication and Exchange Between People or Groups

In its broader, more formal sense, "intercourse" refers to communication, dealings, or interaction between people, communities, or nations. This usage is most common in formal writing, literature, philosophy, history, and diplomacy.

It essentially means: the back-and-forth flow of ideas, trade, culture, or communication between parties.

This sense is often paired with a describing word to clarify what kind of exchange is happening:

  • Social intercourse — everyday conversation and interaction among people in a community. A writer describing life in a small town might say, "The café was the center of social intercourse, where neighbors gathered to talk and share news."
  • Commercial intercourse — the exchange of goods, money, and trade between parties or nations. A history book might say, "The treaty opened the door to free commercial intercourse between the two countries."
  • Diplomatic intercourse — the formal official relationship and communication between governments. "The two nations suspended diplomatic intercourse after the conflict."
  • Intellectual intercourse — the sharing and debating of ideas. "Great universities are built on the free intercourse of ideas."

In all these cases, the emphasis is on mutual, active exchange — not a one-way broadcast, but a genuine two-way relationship between parties.

In its most widely recognized modern sense, "intercourse" — especially when used without any describing word — refers to sexual intercourse, meaning the physical, intimate act of sex between people. In medical, legal, and formal writing, this is the standard, clinical term used instead of informal or vulgar alternatives.

When someone says simply "intercourse" in a modern, everyday conversation, this is almost always the meaning being used.

It can also appear with the modifier to be explicit: "sexual intercourse."
How to Tell Which Sense Is Meant

Context is everything. Ask yourself: What is the subject of the sentence?

  • If the text is about nations, trade, culture, society, or ideas, the general sense is almost certainly intended.
  • If the text is about people's physical or intimate relationship, the sexual sense is almost certainly intended.
  • In older literature (before the 20th century), "intercourse" almost always means the general sense, because that was the dominant usage historically. As the sexual sense became more prominent in everyday speech, the general sense gradually retreated into formal and academic writing.
An Important Shift in Usage Over Time

This is worth knowing as a learner: the general sense is older; the sexual sense has taken over in common speech.

Today, if you say "intercourse" without any qualifying word in a casual conversation, almost every listener will assume you mean the sexual sense. Because of this, most modern writers who want to use the word in its general sense will attach a qualifier — "social intercourse," "commercial intercourse," etc. — to avoid confusion. Without a qualifier in modern everyday language, the sexual meaning is the default assumption.

Both senses share the same fundamental idea: a deep, active, two-way engagement between parties. Whether nations are exchanging trade, people are exchanging ideas, or individuals are physically intimate, the word always implies a genuine, mutual connection — not passive, not one-sided, but a real exchange between two sides. That is the soul of the word.
8943:
Interdependence is the state in which two or more things — people, groups, countries, living creatures, or systems — mutually rely on each other, so that each one needs the others to function, survive, or thrive. It is not a one-way street. It flows in multiple directions at the same time.

Think of it this way: if A needs B, and B also needs A, that relationship between them is called interdependence.
Breaking It Down Simply

The word itself is a clue. It has two parts:

"Inter" means between or among. Think of "international" (between nations) or "interview" (a conversation between people).

"Dependence" means the state of relying on something else.

Put them together: reliance that flows between things. That is interdependence.
The Critical Difference: Dependence vs. Interdependence

This distinction is very important, and many learners miss it.

Dependence is one-directional. A baby depends on its parents for food, warmth, and safety — but the baby does not provide those things back to the parent. That is dependence: one party needs, the other provides.

Interdependence is multi-directional. Both (or all) parties are simultaneously relying on each other. Neither one is purely the "giver" or purely the "receiver." Each one contributes something the other cannot do without.
A Simple, Vivid Example: Bees and Flowers

This is perhaps the clearest example in nature.

Bees need flowers. They fly to flowers to collect nectar, which they use to make food (honey) to feed their colony. Without flowers, bees would starve.

Flowers need bees. When a bee lands on a flower to collect nectar, pollen sticks to its body. When the bee flies to the next flower, that pollen is transferred — a process called pollination — which allows the flower to reproduce. Without bees, most flowering plants could not produce seeds or fruit, and they would eventually die out.

Neither the bee nor the flower is simply the "helper." Each one needs the other. Each one also provides for the other. This two-way, mutual reliance is interdependence.

Notice something important here: if you remove one side, both sides suffer. If bees disappeared, flowers would struggle to reproduce. If flowers disappeared, bees would have no food. The fates of both are tied together. This interconnected vulnerability is a hallmark of interdependence.
A Human Example: The Food on Your Plate

Consider the simple act of eating a piece of bread. Think about everything that had to work together for that bread to reach you.

A farmer grew the wheat. The farmer needed seeds, water, sunlight, and tools — tools made by manufacturers, who needed steel, which was mined by other workers. The wheat was harvested and transported by truck drivers. It went to a mill where workers ground it into flour. The flour went to a bakery, where bakers used electricity (produced by power plant workers) and ovens (built by engineers) to bake the bread. Packagers wrapped it. Delivery drivers moved it to a store. Store workers stocked the shelves. You walked in, paid money you earned by doing your work, and bought the bread.

Every single person in that chain depended on all the others. The farmer could not eat if no one bought the wheat. The truck driver could not work if there was no wheat to transport. The baker could not bake without flour. You could not eat without all of them. All of them could not survive or earn a living without people like you who need bread.

This vast web of mutual reliance — where every participant both gives something and receives something — is interdependence on a massive scale.
Interdependence Between Countries

On a global level, interdependence is why the world's nations are so deeply connected.

Country A might produce oil but lack the technology to build computers. Country B might build excellent computers but have no oil. So Country A sells oil to Country B, and Country B sells computers to Country A. Each country needs the other to get something it cannot easily produce on its own.

This is why events in one part of the world can have ripple effects everywhere else. If a drought destroys the wheat harvest in a major wheat-producing country, bread prices rise globally. If a major country's economy collapses, it can trigger economic difficulties in countries thousands of miles away. Their fates are bound together through interdependence.
Interdependence in Your Own Body

You don't even have to look outside yourself to find a perfect example. Your body is a masterpiece of interdependence.

Your heart pumps blood, which carries oxygen. But your heart needs that oxygen-rich blood to keep its own muscle cells alive. Your lungs bring oxygen into the body — but your lungs need the heart to pump blood to them so they can function. Your stomach digests food and turns it into nutrients — but your stomach needs blood (from the heart) and oxygen (from the lungs) to do its job. Your brain controls everything — but it needs blood, oxygen, and nutrients from all the other organs to keep thinking and controlling.

Remove any one organ, and the entire system — including all the other organs — begins to fail. That total, system-wide mutual reliance is interdependence in its purest form.
Key Qualities of Interdependence

Now that you have seen it in several contexts, here are the defining qualities that are always present whenever true interdependence exists:

Mutuality. All parties in the relationship both give and receive. No one is purely a giver or purely a taker. The reliance is shared.

Connectedness. The parties are linked in such a way that what happens to one has consequences for the others. Their realities overlap.

Shared fate. When one part of an interdependent system is damaged or lost, the rest of the system feels it. The wellbeing of each part is genuinely tied to the wellbeing of the whole.

Balance (usually). In healthy interdependence, there is often a rough balance — each side gets roughly as much as it gives, even if what each side gives is very different in nature. (A bee gives pollination; a flower gives nectar. Very different things, but both parties benefit.)
When Interdependence Is Uneven

Interdependence does not always mean that both sides are equally powerful or equally vulnerable. Sometimes one side depends on the other far more heavily than the other depends on it. This is called asymmetric interdependence.

For example, a small country that exports only one product to a much larger, wealthier country is more vulnerable than that larger country is. If the trade relationship breaks, the small country suffers far more. But both still depend on each other to some degree — there is still interdependence, just unevenly distributed.
Interdependence vs. Independence

It is also worth comparing interdependence to its near-opposite: independence.

Independence means self-sufficiency — not needing others. A person living completely off the land, growing their own food, building their own shelter, and interacting with no one is independent.

Most of the real world, however, is characterized by interdependence rather than independence. The more complex and developed a society or ecosystem is, the more deeply interdependent its parts tend to be — because specialization creates efficiency, and efficiency creates the need to trade and cooperate.
Why Interdependence Matters

Understanding this word matters because it reflects a fundamental truth about how the world actually works. Almost nothing significant operates in true isolation. Families, ecosystems, economies, friendships, democracies, and global systems all function through webs of mutual reliance.

Recognizing interdependence helps you understand:

Why cooperation matters. When you depend on others and others depend on you, working together is not just nice — it is necessary.

Why actions have consequences beyond yourself. Because you are part of interdependent systems, your choices ripple outward and affect others, just as their choices ripple back to affect you.

Why vulnerability is shared. When one part of an interdependent system is weakened — a species goes extinct, a factory shuts down, a country faces crisis — the effects spread, because everything in the system is connected.
One-Line Summary

Interdependence is the condition in which two or more things mutually rely on one another — each needing the other — so that they are bound together by a shared web of give-and-take, and the health of each is inseparable from the health of all.
8944: Interdependent describes two or more things that each depend on the other(s) at the same time. Neither one can fully function, survive, or succeed without the other. The relationship goes both ways — and that "both ways" part is the whole point of the word.

Think of it in three layers:

Dependent means relying on something else. A baby is dependent on its parents.

Independent means not relying on anything else. A self-sufficient farmer who grows their own food is independent.

Interdependent sits in a third, more interesting space. It means: "I need you, and you also need me." Neither party stands alone, and neither party is the only one doing the needing. The dependency is shared, mutual, and two-way (or many-way, when more than two things are involved).

Think of a bee and a flower.

The bee needs the flower — it collects nectar from the flower for food. Without flowers, bees would starve.

The flower needs the bee — when the bee visits, it carries pollen from one flower to another, which is how flowers reproduce. Without bees, many flowers couldn't make seeds and would die out.

So neither the bee nor the flower is simply "dependent" on the other in a one-way sense. They both need each other. They are interdependent.
Another Example: Humans in a City

Think about your daily life in a city. You depend on farmers to grow your food. Farmers depend on truck drivers to deliver supplies. Truck drivers depend on mechanics to fix their vehicles. Mechanics depend on steel workers for parts. Steel workers depend on food from farmers — and the cycle continues.

Every single person in this chain relies on others, and others rely on them. No one person can do everything alone. The whole system is interdependent — each part affects every other part.

For something to be described as interdependent, two things must be true:

1. The dependency is mutual. It is not one person or thing doing all the depending. Both (or all) parties rely on the others. If only one side needs the other, that is simply "dependence," not *inter*dependence.

2. They are still separate things. Interdependent things are distinct — they have their own identity and role. They are not fused into one. A bee and a flower are not the same organism. But they are deeply connected through their need for each other.

Not everything is interdependent to the same degree. Some things are tightly interdependent, meaning if one fails, the other fails quickly and completely. Some things are loosely interdependent, meaning they influence each other but can manage without the other for a while, though not indefinitely or not without cost.

For example:

  • A heart and lungs are tightly interdependent — if the heart stops, the lungs very quickly stop too, and vice versa.
  • Two neighboring countries that trade with each other are interdependent, but perhaps less tightly — if trade slows, both economies suffer, but they do not immediately collapse.

The word "interdependent" covers both tight and loose forms of this mutual reliance.
Where You Will See This Word Used

In nature and science: Ecosystems are described as interdependent because every animal, plant, and organism relies on others in the food chain and environment. Remove one species, and it can ripple through the whole system.

In economics: Countries and businesses are called interdependent when their economies are tied together — what happens in one market affects others. Global trade is a classic example.

In relationships: Two people in a healthy close relationship can be described as interdependent — they support each other, rely on each other emotionally, and each person's wellbeing is genuinely connected to the other's.

In technology: The internet, power grids, and supply chains are all interdependent systems — a failure in one part can cause failures in others.

In politics: Nations in an alliance are interdependent — their security, policies, and decisions affect one another.
How to Spot the Word Being Used Correctly

Ask yourself this test question: "Does each side genuinely need the other?"

If yes → interdependent.
If only one side needs the other → dependent.
If neither needs the other → independent.

For example: "The global economy is interdependent." ✓ — Countries trade with and rely on each other mutually.

"A child is interdependent on its parents." ✗ — This is incorrect usage, because the child needs the parents far more than the parents need the child to survive. It is closer to dependence than *inter*dependence.

Here are the related forms so your understanding is complete:

  • Interdependence (noun) — "The interdependence of species in an ecosystem is remarkable." — This is the state or condition of being interdependent.
  • Interdependently (adverb) — "The two companies operate interdependently." — This describes the way something is done, in a mutually dependent manner.
  • Interdepend (verb, rarely used) — "These systems interdepend." — Simply means to be in a relationship of mutual dependence.
One Final Way to Remember It

Picture a bridge held up by two arches leaning against each other. Neither arch can stand on its own — each one would fall without the other holding it up. But together, they are strong. Each needs the other. That image — two things holding each other up — is the heart of what interdependent means.
8945: An interdict is an official, formal order that prohibits something. Not just a rule or a warning — it is a command issued by a recognised authority that says: "This must stop, or must not happen." The key word is prohibition: an interdict exists to block, ban, or forbid.
The Two Main Worlds Where This Word Lives

The word "interdict" as a noun is used seriously in two distinct areas: law and the Catholic Church. They share the same core idea — a formal prohibition — but they work very differently.

1. The Legal Interdict

In legal systems (particularly in Scotland, South Africa, and several other countries), an interdict is a court order that forbids a person or organisation from doing a specific thing.

A court doesn't just say "please stop." It issues an interdict — a binding, enforceable order. Breaking it is not just wrong; it is contempt of court, meaning the person can be punished by the legal system.

Think of it this way: Imagine your neighbour keeps dumping rubbish on your property. You go to a court. The court issues an interdict against your neighbour, legally ordering them to stop. From that moment, the neighbour has no choice — the law has formally forbidden the action.

You will often see this word in countries that follow a particular legal tradition (Roman-Dutch law or Scots law). In the United States and England, the closest equivalent is called an injunction — it works almost identically. So if you know what an injunction is, a legal interdict is essentially the same thing: a court's formal "stop" order.

An interdict can be:

  • Temporary — issued quickly to stop something urgently, while a full court case is still ongoing.
  • Final — issued permanently after a full court hearing.

2. The Ecclesiastical Interdict (Church)

This is the older and historically more dramatic use of the word. In the Roman Catholic Church, an interdict is a formal Church penalty that bans people from receiving most sacraments and religious rites.

The sacraments — like Holy Communion, marriage in a church, last rites, and Christian burial — are at the centre of Catholic religious life. To be placed under an interdict means you are cut off from these, which in deeply religious times was considered a devastating spiritual punishment.

There are two kinds:

A. Personal Interdict — placed on a specific individual or group of people. That person is forbidden from participating in most Church rites and sacraments. It is serious, but it is less extreme than excommunication (which is the Church's ultimate penalty, meaning full expulsion from the Church community).

B. Local Interdict (or Territorial Interdict) — this is where it gets historically enormous. A local interdict is placed on an entire place — a city, a region, even a whole country. This means no one in that territory can receive the sacraments. No Church masses. No religious marriages. No Christian burials. Churches fall silent. The spiritual life of an entire population is suspended.

Historically, popes wielded local interdicts as powerful political weapons. For example, in 1208, Pope Innocent III placed the entire Kingdom of England under interdict to pressure King John into submission. For the common people of that era — who were deeply Catholic and feared for their souls — this was catastrophic. The psychological and social pressure was immense.

An ecclesiastical interdict is not permanent by nature; it lifts when the punished party complies or makes amends.
Interdict vs. Similar Words — The Important Distinctions

Since you want full clarity, here is how "interdict" sits alongside related words:

Interdict vs. Injunction: In practice, nearly identical in meaning. An injunction is the common term in English law (England, the USA). An interdict is the term used in Scots and Roman-Dutch legal systems (Scotland, South Africa, Zimbabwe, etc.). Both are court orders forbidding something.

Interdict vs. Excommunication: Both are Church penalties, but excommunication is the harsher one. Excommunication removes someone entirely from the Church community. An interdict is less total — the person may still be considered a member of the Church but is forbidden from certain rites and sacraments. Think of excommunication as full expulsion; an interdict as a heavy suspension.

Interdict vs. Ban: A "ban" is an everyday, informal word for any prohibition. An interdict is always formal and official, issued by a court or Church authority, and carries legal or canonical (Church law) force behind it.
The Thread That Ties It All Together

Whether in law or in the Church, an interdict always means the same fundamental thing: a serious, formal, authoritative order of prohibition. It comes from a body with real power — a court or the Church — and it carries consequences if ignored. It is never casual. It is never a suggestion. It is a firm, official stop.
8946:
To interdict something means to officially stop it, forbid it, or cut it off — using the power of authority, law, or force.

It's more than just saying "no." When something is interdicted, a serious power — a court, a military force, a government, a religious institution — actively steps in to make sure it does not happen or cannot continue. There is weight behind it. There is enforcement behind it.

1. Legal and Official: To Forbid by Order

In law and governance, to interdict something means to formally prohibit it through an official ruling, court order, or decree. An authority with legal power draws a hard line and says: this stops now.

"The court interdicted the company from selling the product."
"The government interdicted the import of those chemicals."
"Federal agents interdicted the drug shipment at the border."

Notice that last example — interdicting a shipment is extremely common in law enforcement. It means to officially intercept and stop it from reaching its destination. This is a very frequent real-world use of the word.

2. Military: To Cut Off or Disrupt

In a military context, to interdict means to physically block, disrupt, or destroy an enemy's ability to move, communicate, or receive supplies. This isn't just a legal order — it's an active operation.

Imagine an enemy army moving tanks and food and ammunition along a road. If your air force bombs that road, destroys the bridges, and cuts off the supply chain, you have interdicted those supply lines. You haven't just told the enemy they can't move — you have made it impossible.

"The air force was tasked with interdicting enemy supply routes."
"The navy interdicted the vessel before it reached port."

The key idea here: you are severing, blocking, or disrupting — physically preventing movement or access.

3. Ecclesiastical (Church): To Bar from Religious Rites

Historically, the Catholic Church used this word to describe a formal punishment where a person or an entire region was barred from participating in sacred rites and sacraments. A priest could be interdicted — stripped of his right to perform his duties. A whole city or kingdom could be placed under an interdict, meaning no masses, no baptisms, no Christian burials could take place there.

"The Pope interdicted the kingdom until the king complied."
"The bishop interdicted the rebellious priest."

This sense is rare in everyday modern language, but you will encounter it in history books and religious texts.
What Makes "Interdict" Different from Similar Words

"Forbid," "prohibit," and "interdict" all involve saying no, but they are not the same:

Forbid is personal and informal. A mother forbids her child from leaving the house. A friend forbids you from telling a secret. No formal authority is needed.

Prohibit is what rules and laws do. Speed limits prohibit driving too fast. Laws prohibit theft. It's impersonal and rule-based, but it doesn't necessarily imply active enforcement.

Interdict goes further. It implies:

  • A powerful, formal authority is the one doing the stopping
  • There is often active enforcement — not just a rule on paper, but a physical or legal mechanism making sure the thing cannot happen
  • The action being stopped is usually significant — shipments, military movements, a person's rights, a legal transaction

You would never say "my teacher interdicted me from chewing gum." That would sound absurd. But you would say "the court interdicted the merger" or "special forces interdicted the weapons convoy."

"Interdict" is a formal, serious word. It belongs in courtrooms, military briefings, government documents, and historical accounts. You will rarely hear it in casual conversation. When a writer or speaker chooses "interdict" over "stop" or "forbid," they are signaling gravity — something official and authoritative is happening.

To interdict is to officially and authoritatively stop something — whether through a legal order, military force, or institutional power. Depending on the context:

  • In law: a court or government formally prohibits something or seizes/stops a shipment
  • In the military: forces physically cut off an enemy's movement, supplies, or communications
  • In church history: a religious authority bars a person or place from religious participation

The thread connecting all three: a serious power actively preventing something from happening or continuing.
8947:
Interdiction means the official act of stopping, blocking, or forbidding something. Think of it as a powerful, authoritative barrier — whether physical or legal — placed in the path of something to prevent it from continuing.

The key word here is official. Interdiction is never just any random act of stopping. It is always carried out by someone in a position of authority — a government, a military force, a court, a law enforcement agency. That authority is baked into the word.
The Three Main Contexts You'll Encounter It In

The word "interdiction" is used across three main areas of life. Understanding all three will give you complete command of the word.

1. Law and Government — Forbidding Something by Order

In a legal or governmental context, interdiction means a formal, official order that prohibits something from happening or that restricts a person's legal rights and freedoms.

For example, a court might issue an interdiction against a person, meaning they are legally barred from doing certain things — such as managing their own finances, making legal decisions, or being in a certain place. It is similar to a court injunction or a restraining order — it is a legal wall built around a person or an action.

Think of it this way: if a judge says "you are forbidden, by the authority of this court," that act of forbidding — and the order itself — is the interdiction.

2. Military — Cutting Off the Enemy

This is one of the most widely used meanings of the word, especially in military history and strategy.

In warfare, interdiction means the deliberate action of attacking or blocking the enemy's ability to move, communicate, or receive supplies. The goal is not necessarily to destroy the enemy directly, but to cut them off — from their reinforcements, their food, their weapons, their routes of travel.

For example, if an air force bombs a series of bridges and roads behind enemy lines so that enemy soldiers cannot receive fresh troops or ammunition, that is called air interdiction. The military is "interdicting" — intercepting and shutting down — the flow of resources to the enemy.

Picture a tree being cut off from its roots. The tree doesn't die instantly, but it will eventually. Military interdiction works on that same principle: starve the enemy of what they need until they are weakened or stopped.

3. Law Enforcement — Intercepting Illegal Activity

In policing and border control, interdiction refers to the act of intercepting and seizing illegal goods — most commonly drugs, weapons, or contraband — before they reach their destination.

You will often hear phrases like drug interdiction or border interdiction. This describes the work of agencies like the coast guard, customs officers, or narcotics police who actively patrol routes, seas, and borders to intercept and stop illegal shipments.

Here, the word captures both the physical act of interception and the authority behind it. It is not a random citizen confiscating something; it is an authorised force blocking an illegal flow.

No matter which context you see it in, interdiction always carries the same DNA:

  • There is something in motion or about to happen (a person's action, a military supply line, a drug shipment, a legal activity).
  • Someone in authority steps in.
  • That authority blocks, stops, or forbids it.

That is interdiction — an authoritative act of stopping or blocking.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Prohibition is close in meaning, but it tends to focus on the rule or law itself ("alcohol prohibition"). Interdiction focuses more on the active act of stopping or blocking — it implies intervention, not just a standing rule.

Ban is a simpler, more casual word. Interdiction carries weight and formality. You would say a government bans plastic bags, but a court issues an interdiction against a person's actions.

Interception is about catching something mid-way. Interdiction includes interception but is broader — it can also mean a standing legal prohibition, not just a single catch.

• "The navy conducted an interdiction of vessels suspected of carrying illegal weapons."
  • "The court placed the elderly man under interdiction after he was found incapable of managing his own affairs."
  • "Allied air interdiction campaigns destroyed supply routes, crippling the enemy's ability to fight."
  • "The coast guard's drug interdiction unit seized over two tonnes of cocaine last year."
Interdiction is the official act — by a court, a military, or a law enforcement body — of stopping, blocking, or forbidding something from happening, moving, or continuing.
8948: A discipline is a field of study — like biology, history, psychology, mathematics, economics, or engineering. Each one has its own questions it tries to answer, its own tools and methods, and its own body of knowledge. Biologists study living things. Historians study the past. Economists study money, markets, and human decisions. In academic and professional life, these fields generally stay within their own boundaries.

Interdisciplinary is an adjective that describes something — a project, a course, a team, a research effort, an approach — that involves, combines, or integrates two or more different disciplines to understand a problem or create something new.

The prefix inter- carries the meaning of "between" or "among," so the word captures the idea of something existing or happening between disciplines, bridging them rather than staying locked inside just one.

The most important word in understanding this is integration. It's not enough to simply mention biology and then separately mention psychology. Interdisciplinary means those fields are actively working with each other, where insights from one genuinely shape, challenge, or enrich the other.
A picture that makes it click

Imagine a large building where every discipline is a separate room. Biologists work in Room 1. Psychologists work in Room 2. Sociologists work in Room 3. Normally, experts stay in their own room and solve problems using only the tools available there.

An interdisciplinary approach is like knocking down the walls between rooms and letting the people — and their tools and ideas — come together to work on a problem that no single room could solve alone.

Climate change is a classic interdisciplinary challenge. Understanding it fully requires physics (how heat behaves), chemistry (how greenhouse gases work), ecology (how ecosystems respond), economics (the cost of solutions), political science (how policies get made), and psychology (why people resist changing their behavior). No single discipline owns the whole problem, and no single discipline can fix it. The fields must work together — which is precisely what makes climate science interdisciplinary.

Neuroscience is an interdisciplinary field — meaning the field itself was born from the merging of biology, chemistry, psychology, physics, and computer science to understand how the brain works. None of those fields alone could build the complete picture.

Designing a hospital building requires architectural design (aesthetics, function), structural engineering (safety, stability), environmental science (ventilation, infection control), psychology (how spaces affect patient recovery), and social science (how staff and patients move and interact). Pull any one of those out and the design suffers.

Addressing teenage mental health involves psychology, neuroscience, sociology, education, economics, and public health — all at once.
Why it matters: the core idea behind the word

Some problems are too big, too messy, or too layered for any one field to handle. Interdisciplinary thinking exists as a response to that reality. It is an act of intellectual humility — an acknowledgment that different fields have different lenses, and that the most complete understanding comes from combining them.

It is also about producing something new. When disciplines genuinely integrate, the result is often a method, a solution, or an insight that wouldn't have been possible within any single field working alone.

Because it is an adjective, "interdisciplinary" always modifies a noun. Here are the most natural and common pairings:

  • interdisciplinary research — research that draws meaningfully on multiple fields
  • interdisciplinary approach — a way of tackling a problem by combining fields
  • interdisciplinary team — a group of experts from different disciplines working together
  • interdisciplinary studies — a course or program that formally blends disciplines
  • interdisciplinary collaboration — cooperative work that crosses field boundaries
  • interdisciplinary field — a field that is itself built on the integration of several disciplines

Some example sentences showing natural usage:

"The university launched an interdisciplinary program combining medicine and data science to improve cancer diagnosis."

"Solving urban homelessness requires an interdisciplinary approach that draws on sociology, economics, urban planning, and mental health services."

"She joined an interdisciplinary research team to study how social media affects adolescent brain development."

"The course is designed to give students an interdisciplinary perspective on environmental policy."
What it is NOT — important distinctions

You will often encounter two closely related words: multidisciplinary and transdisciplinary. Knowing the difference between them sharpens your understanding of "interdisciplinary" significantly.

Multidisciplinary means that multiple disciplines are brought together and used side by side, but each still works mostly within its own boundaries. A multidisciplinary team working on a patient might have a doctor, a dietitian, and a social worker each contributing their own separate report — but they don't necessarily reshape each other's thinking. The fields stay parallel.

Interdisciplinary means the disciplines genuinely interact and integrate. Knowledge from one field actually changes how another field approaches the problem. A biologist and a psychologist don't just work next to each other — their ideas merge and challenge each other to produce something neither could reach alone.

Transdisciplinary goes even further. Here, the disciplines blend so deeply that a completely new framework emerges — one that doesn't "belong" to any of the original fields. It transcends the boundaries altogether.

Think of it as a spectrum: multidisciplinary (parallel, side by side) → interdisciplinary (crossing and integrating) → transdisciplinary (merging into something entirely new).

In everyday life, people often use "multidisciplinary" and "interdisciplinary" interchangeably, and that's fine in casual use. But in academic and professional contexts, the distinction above is the careful and precise one.

Cross-disciplinary is another term you'll see and it generally means the same thing as interdisciplinary — working across the boundaries of fields.
Register: when and where you'll encounter this word

"Interdisciplinary" is a formal, academic word. You'll find it most commonly in university course catalogs and degree programs, academic research papers and grant applications, professional fields like healthcare, public policy, and scientific research, and any intellectual writing that discusses how knowledge is organized or applied.

It signals complexity, seriousness, and a recognition that real-world problems don't respect the neat borders that academic fields draw around themselves. When someone calls a project or approach interdisciplinary, they are saying: this problem is rich enough — and important enough — that it deserves more than one way of thinking.
The complete picture in one place

Interdisciplinary (adjective) describes anything that deliberately involves the integration of two or more academic or professional disciplines to address a question, solve a problem, or build understanding that would be incomplete — or impossible — within any single field alone. Its defining quality is genuine integration, not just the presence of multiple subjects. When fields are truly interdisciplinary, they borrow from each other, challenge each other, and together produce insights that none of them could have reached on their own.
8949:
When you use interest as a verb, it means to cause a feeling of curiosity, attention, or engagement in someone. In other words, something interests you when it makes you want to know more, look closer, or pay attention to it.

Think of it this way: the verb "interest" is about creating a feeling inside a person. Something acts on you, and as a result, you feel drawn toward it.

"History interests me."
→ History creates that feeling of curiosity inside me. It pulls me in.
The Key Idea: It Is a Causative Verb

This is the most important thing to understand. The verb interest is causative — it means to cause interest. The subject of the sentence is not feeling something; the subject is producing a feeling in someone else.

Look at this carefully:

"The documentary interested the students."

Here, the documentary is doing something to the students. It is causing a feeling of curiosity and engagement in them. The students are the ones receiving that feeling.

This is why you will always find a person (or a group of people) as the object of this verb. Something interests someone. That someone is always on the receiving end.
The Two Main Ways "Interest" Is Used as a Verb

Pattern 1: Something interests someone

[Thing] + interest + [Person]

This is the most common pattern. A thing — a topic, an idea, a story, an object — causes a feeling of curiosity or engagement in a person.

  • "Science interests her deeply."
  • "Not many things interest him these days."
  • "What interests you most about this course?"
  • "The case interested the detective."
  • "Very few books interest young children as much as picture books do."

Notice that the thing doing the "interesting" doesn't have to be exciting or dramatic. It just has to create some level of curiosity or attention in the person.

Pattern 2: To interest someone in something

[Person/Thing] + interest + [Person] + in + [Something]

Here, someone (or something) tries to make another person want to be involved in, try, or buy something. This pattern carries a slight sense of persuasion — you are attempting to spark someone's interest in a particular thing.

  • "Can I interest you in a cup of tea?"
    → Can I make you want a cup of tea? Would you like one?
  • "She interested her younger brother in painting."
    → She made him want to try painting. She sparked that interest in him.
  • "The salesperson tried to interest the customer in a newer model."
    → The salesperson tried to make the customer curious about and wanting the newer model.
  • "The teacher interested her students in local history by taking them on field trips."

This second pattern is especially common in polite offers and sales situations. "Can I interest you in...?" is a very standard, slightly formal way of offering something to someone.

The verb interest sits in the middle of the emotional spectrum. It doesn't mean to excite, thrill, or fascinate — those are stronger. It doesn't mean to merely inform. It means something has genuinely caught someone's attention and made them want to engage more.

You can add adverbs to show the degree:

  • "The subject barely interests me." (very low engagement)
  • "The subject interests me quite a bit." (moderate engagement)
  • "The subject deeply interests me." (strong, genuine curiosity)
A Common Source of Confusion: "Interest" vs. "Be Interested"

Learners often mix up these two, so it's worth being clear.

"The topic interests me." → The topic is actively causing a feeling in me. The topic is doing something. (Verb)

"I am interested in the topic." → I am in a state of feeling interest. The focus is on my feeling. (Adjective)

Both sentences communicate a similar idea, but the angle is different. In the first, the topic is the actor. In the second, you are describing your own state of mind. Both are perfectly correct and natural.

Similarly:

  • "The story interests me." → The story does something to me.
  • "I am interested in the story." → I have that feeling.

In everyday speech, both forms are used, but "be interested in" is more conversational and far more common. The verb form "interests" sounds slightly more formal or literary.

Like any verb, interest works naturally in negatives and questions:

Negatives:

  • "Nothing interests him anymore." (He has lost all curiosity for things.)
  • "The offer didn't interest her at all."

Questions:

  • "Does this interest you?"
  • "What interests you about medicine?"
  • "Would it interest you to hear more?"
Important Thing to Remember About Tense

The simple present tense of interest is used to describe ongoing, general states — not actions happening right now.

  • ✅ "Art interests me." (This is a general truth about you.)
  • ❌ "Art is interesting me." (This is unnatural and almost never used.)

Just like the verb love or know, the verb interest (when describing a general feeling) is not normally used in the continuous (-ing) form in standard English.

To interest someone means to cause a feeling of curiosity and engagement in them. Something reaches inside a person and makes them want to pay attention, learn more, or get involved. It is always the thing that interests, and always the person who receives that feeling. You can also use it to mean trying to make someone want something, especially in polite offers.
8950:
An interface is the point, surface, or system where two separate things meet and interact. It is the shared boundary between two distinct sides — the "in between."

Picture a glass of water sitting open to the air. Where the water ends and the air begins, there is a thin surface — a dividing line between two completely different substances. That dividing line, where those two substances meet and interact, is an interface. It belongs to neither the water nor the air. It is the boundary between them.

This is the soul of the word, and it never changes no matter what field you encounter it in: an interface is a point of contact between two distinct things, where some form of exchange or interaction takes place.

You encounter interfaces constantly without realizing it.

The keyboard you type on is an interface between you and your computer. The steering wheel of a car is an interface between the driver and the vehicle. The buttons on a TV remote are an interface. The touchscreen of a smartphone is an interface between your fingers and the software inside.

In every case, notice the pattern: there are two parties — a person and a machine, or two different systems — and the interface is what sits between them, making communication possible. Remove the interface, and the two sides can no longer connect.

In science, "interface" specifically refers to the physical boundary between two different substances or states of matter.

The surface of the ocean, where seawater meets air, is a liquid-gas interface. The boundary between a rock and the water flowing over it is a solid-liquid interface. Scientists study these boundaries carefully because some of the most important chemical and physical reactions happen at the interface — not inside either substance, but right at the boundary between them.

The most common place you will hear "interface" today is in computing. A user interface — often shortened to UI — is everything you see and interact with on a device: the buttons, menus, icons, sliders, text fields, and screens that allow you to communicate with a computer or app.

Think of the UI as a translator. Deep inside a computer, everything is electrical signals and binary code — utterly unintelligible to a human. The user interface takes all of that and presents it to you in a form you understand (visuals, text, sounds), while also translating your human actions (taps, clicks, swipes) into signals the computer can process. Neither side needs to speak the other's raw language — the interface handles the translation.

There are different kinds of user interfaces, depending on how interaction happens:

A graphical user interface (GUI) — pronounced "gooey" — is what almost every modern device uses. It presents visual, clickable elements: icons you tap, windows you drag, menus you scroll through. When you open an app by tapping its icon, you are using a GUI.

A command-line interface (CLI) is a text-only interface where you type written commands rather than clicking on visuals. It has no graphics — just text in and text out. Programmers and system administrators use these regularly because they offer precise, powerful control.

A voice interface is one where spoken language is the input. When you speak to a virtual assistant, you are using a voice interface.

All of these are still interfaces in the same sense — a layer that sits between a human and a machine, making communication possible in both directions.
In Technology: The API (Application Programming Interface)

Not every interface is between a human and a machine. Sometimes, two computer programs need to communicate with each other — and the interface that makes this possible is called an API, which stands for Application Programming Interface.

An API is a defined set of rules that specifies how one program can make a request to another program, and what kind of response it will receive in return.

A helpful analogy: imagine you are a customer in a restaurant. You do not walk into the kitchen and cook the food yourself — you do not even need to know how the kitchen works. Instead, you speak to a waiter, who takes your order to the kitchen using a standard process and brings your food back. The waiter — along with the whole formal system of menus, order slips, and serving protocols — is the interface between you and the kitchen.

An API works exactly this way. When a weather app on your phone shows you today's forecast, it almost certainly did not collect that weather data itself. It sent a request through a weather company's API — something like "give me the current temperature for this city" — and the API responded with the data. The app never needed to know how the weather company's servers work internally. It only needed to know the rules of the API.

This is the great power of an API: it lets two programs cooperate without either one needing to understand the internal workings of the other. They only need to agree on the rules of their shared interface.

Interfaces also exist in the physical, tangible world of hardware.

A USB port is a hardware interface — a standardized physical connection point that allows two devices (say, a laptop and a flash drive) to plug together and exchange data. HDMI ports, headphone jacks, and charging ports are all hardware interfaces. Each one is a carefully standardized boundary point, designed so that any two compatible devices can connect and communicate through it.

The standardization is crucial. Because USB follows a universal standard, any USB device can connect to any USB port, regardless of who made either one. The interface is the agreed-upon contract between them.
In Programming: Interface as a Contract

In software development — especially in languages like Java and C# — the word "interface" takes on a more specific, technical meaning, though it is still rooted in the same core idea.

Here, an interface is a formal agreement, or contract, written in code. It says: "Any piece of code that wants to play this role must be capable of doing these specific things." It lists the exact actions (called methods) that must be supported — without specifying how each action is carried out.

An analogy: imagine you are hiring for a delivery driver position. You don't care whether a driver uses a bicycle, a van, or a motorbike. You only care that they can do three things: pick up a package, deliver a package, and confirm delivery. You have defined the requirements of the role without dictating how each driver fulfills them.

In programming, an interface works identically. Different pieces of code can each fulfill (or "implement") the interface in their own way, as long as they all support the required actions. This makes large software systems far more flexible — different components built by different teams at different times can still work together seamlessly, as long as they all respect the same interface.
The One Thread Running Through Everything

Across science, everyday life, hardware, software, and programming, the word "interface" always means essentially the same thing.

An interface is never one of the two parties. It is always what sits between them. It is the bridge, the translator, the agreed-upon meeting point. It defines the rules of engagement between two distinct sides — whether those sides are water and air, a human and a computer, two apps exchanging data, two hardware devices plugged together, or code modules cooperating inside a program.

If you remember one thing: an interface is the point of connection between two different things, where communication or interaction is made possible.
8951:
To interface means to connect with something or someone in a way that allows communication, exchange, or cooperation to happen between two distinct things.

Think of it this way: when two things that are separate — two systems, two groups, two devices, or two people — need to work together, they interface with each other. The word focuses on the point of contact and interaction between them, not just the fact that they met.

You almost always see it used as:

"to interface with" something or someone.

You don't usually say "they interfaced each other." You say "they interfaced with each other."
What Makes It Different From "Connect" or "Talk"

This is important. You could sometimes replace "interface" with words like connect, interact, communicate, or work with — and the sentence would still make sense. So why use "interface"?

Because "interface" carries a more specific and structured meaning. It implies:

  • The two things involved are distinct from each other — they have their own separate identities, systems, or roles.
  • The connection between them is purposeful and functional — something is actually being exchanged or achieved through this connection.
  • There is often a defined boundary or channel through which the interaction happens.

So "interface" is not just casual contact. It suggests a deliberate, structured, functional interaction between two separate entities.

The verb is used in both technical and non-technical settings.

1. Technology and Computers

This is where you'll most commonly encounter it.

"This new software interfaces with the company's existing database."

Here, the software and the database are two separate systems. "Interfaces with" tells you they connect at a specific point and exchange data in a structured way. It's not just that they exist near each other — they actively communicate and cooperate.

"The device interfaces with your smartphone via Bluetooth."

Two separate devices. One connection point. Information flows between them.

2. Business and Organizations

"The project manager interfaces with both the engineering team and the clients."

The project manager sits between two groups and serves as the connection point — passing information, aligning expectations, and enabling cooperation between people who don't directly talk to each other. This is a very common use in professional and corporate environments.

"Our department interfaces directly with the legal team whenever a contract is involved."

Again — two separate departments, coming together at a defined point for a specific purpose.

3. Science and Engineering

"The new electrode is designed to interface with living tissue."

A device and biological tissue — two very different things — are being connected in a functional way. The word handles this kind of unusual pairing naturally.

4. General / Everyday Use

"As a teacher, she interfaces with students, parents, and administrators every single day."

Here it means she regularly connects and communicates with all three groups as part of her role. The word gives a sense that these are structured, role-based interactions — not just casual chats.

"Interface" carries a slightly formal, professional, or technical tone. It is not a word you'd typically use in casual conversation with a friend. You wouldn't say, "I interfaced with my brother last night" — that would sound unnatural. You'd just say "I spoke to my brother."

But in a workplace, a technical report, a scientific paper, or a business presentation, "interface" fits perfectly because it signals that the interaction is structured and functional, not just social.

FormExample
Base formto interface
Present (third person)It interfaces with the system.
Past tenseThey interfaced with the client last week.
Present participleShe is interfacing with the team right now.
A Simple Test to Know When to Use It

Ask yourself: Are two separate things connecting at a specific point for a functional, purposeful exchange?

  • If yes → "interface" works perfectly.
  • If the connection is casual, informal, or not structured → choose "talk," "meet," or "connect" instead.
To interface with something means to connect and interact with it in a structured, purposeful way — allowing two distinct things to communicate, exchange information, or work together.
8952:
Interfere means to get involved in something in a way that causes disruption, problems, or is simply unwanted.

Think of it this way: imagine two things that are going along smoothly — a person living their life, a machine doing its job, a plan being executed — and then something comes along and gets in the way, disturbing that smooth flow. That "getting in the way" is interference.

There are two main situations where you use this word, and understanding both is key.
Situation 1: Interfering in someone's affairs (people and human situations)

This is when a person gets involved in a situation that is not their business, without being asked, and in a way that the other person finds unwanted or annoying.

The key feeling here is: you had no right to get involved, but you did anyway.

Examples:

  • "My neighbour keeps interfering in my marriage." → She involves herself in your relationship, gives unsolicited opinions, and stirs things up.
  • "The government should not interfere in people's private lives." → The government shouldn't involve itself in decisions that belong to individuals.
  • "Stop interfering! I can handle this myself." → Back off — your involvement is unwelcome.
  • "He always interferes whenever his adult children have an argument." → He jumps in when no one asked him to.

Notice the preposition used here is "in" — you interfere in a situation, a conflict, someone's affairs, someone's relationship, someone's decisions.
Situation 2: Interfering with something (disrupting or blocking)

This is when something gets in the way of another thing and prevents it from working properly, happening correctly, or continuing smoothly. The focus here is less about a nosy person and more about something obstructing or disrupting a process, function, or plan.

Examples:

  • "The loud construction noise interferes with my ability to concentrate." → The noise gets in the way of concentration; it makes concentration difficult or impossible.
  • "Heavy cloud cover interfered with the satellite signal." → The clouds blocked or disrupted the signal.
  • "Stress can interfere with sleep." → Stress disrupts the normal process of sleeping.
  • "The injury interfered with his training schedule." → It got in the way and disrupted his plans.
  • "Don't let personal feelings interfere with your professional judgement." → Don't let emotions disrupt or cloud your professional thinking.

The preposition here is "with" — you interfere with a plan, a process, a signal, someone's work, someone's sleep, someone's rights.
The Critical Distinction: "Interfere IN" vs "Interfere WITH"

This is one of the most important nuances of this word.

Interfere INUsed when a person gets involved in a human situation (affairs, decisions, relationships, conflicts) without being invited or wanted.
Interfere WITHUsed when something (a person, a thing, an event) disrupts, obstructs, or blocks something from working or happening properly.
  • "She interfered in my business decisions." → She got involved where she shouldn't have.
  • "Her constant calls interfered with my ability to focus on my business decisions." → Her calls disrupted my concentration and blocked me from working well.

Both are negative, but the angle is different. "In" = unwanted involvement. "With" = disruption or obstruction.
The Tone and Feeling of the Word

Interfere is almost always negative. It carries the sense that something is happening that should not be happening — that the involvement or disruption is harmful, unwelcome, or inappropriate.

You will rarely, if ever, use "interfere" to describe something positive. Compare:

  • "She interfered in my life." → Negative. She overstepped.
  • "She helped me with my life." → Positive. She was welcome.

If someone accuses you of interfering, they are saying you overstepped a boundary, that your involvement was not wanted, and that you may have made things worse rather than better. It is a word of complaint, criticism, and objection.
A Special, Serious Use: "Interfere with a person"

In legal and formal language — especially in British English — "interfere with" someone can be a serious euphemism meaning to sexually assault or molest someone, particularly a child. For example, you might read in a legal context: "He was charged with interfering with a minor."

This use is formal and legal in register. You would not use it in casual conversation to mean sexual assault — in ordinary speech, people would use more direct language. But you must know this meaning exists so that if you encounter it in a news report, legal document, or serious writing, you are not confused.
Common Collocations (Words that Often Appear With "Interfere")

Getting familiar with what words are commonly used alongside interfere will make it much easier to use naturally.

Interfere IN: someone's affairs, someone's life, someone's relationship, someone's decisions, someone's business, a dispute, a conflict, domestic matters, politics.

Interfere WITH: someone's plans, someone's work, someone's concentration, someone's sleep, someone's rights, a signal, a process, normal functioning, the investigation, the schedule, one's judgement, one's duties.
Synonyms — and Why "Interfere" Is Uniquely Strong

Knowing similar words helps you sharpen your understanding of what interfere specifically means.

For Situation 1 (getting involved uninvited):

  • Meddle — Very close in meaning. To meddle is to interfere in other people's affairs in a way that is nosy and clumsy. (She's always meddling.) Slightly more informal than interfere.
  • Intrude — To enter a space or situation where you are not welcome. Focuses more on the act of entry itself.
  • Butt in — Informal. To jump into a conversation or situation uninvited.
  • Poke your nose in — Informal. To be nosy and get involved where you don't belong.

Interfere is the most formal and serious-sounding of these. It also covers a wider range of situations — both human affairs and physical disruption.

For Situation 2 (disruption/obstruction):

  • Disrupt — To break the normal flow of something. (The protest disrupted traffic.)
  • Hinder — To make it harder for something to happen or someone to do something. (Bad weather hindered the rescue efforts.)
  • Obstruct — To block. (The truck obstructed the road.)
  • Hamper — To make something difficult by getting in the way. (Lack of funding hampered the project.)

Among these, interfere is special because it implies not just difficulty, but an active getting in the way — something that shouldn't be there is there, causing the disruption.

To be precise, it's worth being clear on what the word doesn't mean:

  • It does not simply mean to help or to get involved in a neutral sense. Getting involved is only "interfering" when that involvement is unwanted, disruptive, or harmful.
  • It does not mean to cause something to happen. It means to prevent or disrupt something from happening (or to get involved where you shouldn't). The effect of interference is almost always negative for the thing being interfered with.

If you had to carry one clear image in your mind for "interfere," picture this:

A river flowing smoothly. Someone throws a large rock into the middle of it. Now the water is disturbed — it flows awkwardly, splashes in wrong directions, and the smooth current is broken. The rock interfered with the river.

Or picture:

Two people having a private conversation to resolve their disagreement. A third person pushes in between them, starts talking loudly, and gives their own opinion without being asked. That person interfered in their conversation.

In both cases, something was going along on its own — and something else came along and disturbed it, blocked it, or overstepped into it. That is the essence of interfere.
8953:
Imagine a river flowing smoothly. Now imagine someone throws a large rock into the middle of it. The rock doesn't stop the river entirely, but it gets in the way — it disrupts the flow, changes the direction, and makes things more difficult.

That rock is interfering with the river.

This is the heart of the phrase: to interfere with something means to get involved with it in a way that disrupts, hinders, blocks, or damages it — usually in a way that is unwanted.

The key word here is unwanted. When you interfere with something, you are not invited. You push your way into a process, a situation, or an object, and as a result, things don't go the way they were supposed to go.

"Interfere" comes from a Latin root meaning to strike between — to push yourself between two things. Think of it as putting yourself in the middle where you don't belong.

"With" connects the action to its target. It tells you what is being disrupted.

So the full phrase means: to strike between [something] and its normal, intended outcome.
The Different Ways It Is Used

The phrase "interfere with" works across many situations. Here are all the major ones:

1. Disrupting a Process or Activity

This is the most common use. Something — a noise, a distraction, an obstacle — gets in the way of a process that was trying to happen smoothly.

"The loud music interfered with my studying."

Here, the music came between you and your ability to study. It didn't make studying completely impossible, but it made it harder and less effective.

More examples:

  • "The bad weather interfered with the flight schedule."
  • "His injury interfered with his training."
  • "Stress can interfere with sleep."

Notice that in each case, something was happening (studying, flights, training, sleep) and something else pushed in and disturbed it.

2. Meddling in Someone Else's Affairs

When a person involves themselves in a situation that is not their business — especially when they do so in a way that causes trouble — they are interfering with it.

"Please don't interfere with how I manage my team."
"She always interferes with her adult children's decisions."
"The government should not interfere with citizens' personal freedoms."

In this use, the person doing the interfering has no right or invitation to be involved. They push their way in, and things get worse or more complicated as a result.

3. Tampering With an Object or System

When someone physically touches, adjusts, or damages something they are not supposed to touch, they are interfering with it.

"Do not interfere with the equipment."
"Someone had interfered with the lock on the door."
"Interfering with the machinery could cause serious damage."

This is common in warnings and instructions. The message is: keep your hands off and let the thing function as it should.

4. Legal Contexts (Obstruction and Tampering)

In law, "interfere with" is used very specifically to mean obstructing or tampering with a legal process, person, or institution.

"He was charged with interfering with a witness."
"It is illegal to interfere with the course of justice."
"She was accused of interfering with the investigation."

This is a serious use. It means someone deliberately got in the way of something that the law was trying to accomplish.

5. Technical and Scientific Contexts

In science, particularly physics, "interfere with" describes what happens when two waves (like light waves, sound waves, or radio waves) meet and affect each other.

"The radio signal was interfering with the television reception."
"The two light waves interfered with each other and cancelled out."

Even in this technical sense, the core idea holds: something is getting in the way of something else and disturbing its behaviour.

6. A Legal Euphemism (Important to Know)

In legal and formal language — particularly when talking about crimes against children — "interfere with" is sometimes used as a careful, indirect way to refer to sexual abuse or assault.

"The man was convicted of interfering with a minor."

You should be aware of this use so that when you read it in a legal document, a news article, or a formal report, you understand exactly what is being said. This use is always serious and always refers to a crime.

This phrase is what linguists call a prepositional verb — a verb ("interfere") that is paired with a preposition ("with") to create a specific meaning.

It always needs an object. You cannot say "he interfered with" and leave it there — you must say what he interfered with:

✅ "He interfered with the experiment."
❌ "He interfered with." (This is incomplete and incorrect.)

It is almost always used in the negative or to describe a problem. You rarely say "interfere with" in a neutral or positive way. The phrase itself carries a sense that something has gone wrong.

This is a small but important distinction.

"Interfere with" targets a specific thing, process, or person — it disrupts it.

"Don't interfere with the machine."
"The noise interfered with my concentration."

"Interfere in" means to get involved in a situation or matter — especially someone else's affairs.

"Don't interfere in our argument."
"Other countries should not interfere in our politics."

The difference is subtle. Think of it this way: "with" targets a thing or process directly; "in" targets a situation or domain. Both carry the sense of unwanted involvement, but "interfere in" is more about getting into affairs that are not yours, while "interfere with" is more about disrupting something specific.

In practice, many native speakers use the two interchangeably in casual speech, but in formal or precise writing, the distinction matters.
The Tone and Feel of the Phrase

"Interfere with" almost always carries a negative tone. It suggests:

  • Something is being disrupted.
  • The disruption is unwanted.
  • The result is that something works less well than it should, or is damaged or corrupted.

When someone says "stop interfering with that," the message is clear: you are making things worse. Step back and let things proceed naturally.

——

To put it in one clear sentence:

"Interfere with" means to get involved with something in a way that is not wanted, and that disrupts, hinders, damages, or prevents it from working or happening as it should.

Whether it is a noise interfering with your focus, a person meddling in your business, someone tampering with a machine, or a legal obstruction — the idea is always the same: something has pushed its way in, uninvited, and made things worse.
8954:
Interference means getting in the way of something — disrupting it, blocking it, or meddling in it in a way that disturbs whatever was already happening.

Picture a train running smoothly on its track. Now someone drops a heavy object on the track. That object is interfering with the train's journey. It doesn't matter whether it happened on purpose or by accident — the key idea is that something stepped in and disturbed a process that was already in motion.

No matter where you encounter this word, three things are always present:

  1. Something was happening — a process, a signal, a plan, a right, an activity.
  2. Something else got in the way — a person, a force, a signal, an object.
  3. The first thing was disrupted, blocked, or distorted as a result.

That three-part pattern is the soul of the word. Keep it in mind and every use of "interference" will instantly make sense to you.
The Everyday Meaning — Meddling in Someone Else's Affairs

This is the most common way people use the word in daily life. It means getting involved in something that isn't your business, especially when your involvement is unwelcome and causes problems.

"My boss resented the CEO's interference in her department's decisions."
"She wanted to handle it herself, without interference from her family."
"The country accused its neighbor of interference in its internal politics."

In this sense, interference almost always carries a negative tone. It implies the person interfering is overstepping a boundary — going where they don't belong. There is an important distinction to keep in mind here: if someone asks you to get involved, your involvement is called help or assistance. If you push your way in without being invited, that is interference.

This is a scientific meaning, but it is worth understanding because it appears frequently.

In physics, interference refers to what happens when two or more waves — such as sound waves, light waves, or water waves — meet and interact with each other.

When waves meet, they don't bounce off each other like billiard balls. Instead, they combine, and two things can happen depending on how they line up:

Constructive interference happens when the waves line up peak-to-peak. They add together and create a larger, stronger wave. Think of two small ripples in a pond meeting and merging into one bigger ripple.

Destructive interference happens when the waves are misaligned — peak meets trough — and they cancel each other out, producing a weaker wave or even complete silence. This is exactly how noise-canceling headphones work: the headphones generate a sound wave that is the perfect mirror-opposite of the surrounding noise, so the two waves wipe each other out, and you hear quiet.

"The alternating bright and dark bands on the screen were produced by the interference of two light beams."
"Noise-canceling headphones rely on destructive interference to block background sound."

Notice that in physics, interference is not inherently good or bad — it is simply what waves naturally do when they meet.
In Communication and Technology — Signal Interference

When you are listening to the radio and hear crackling, static, or another station bleeding in — that is interference. When your Wi-Fi signal weakens because your microwave is running nearby — that is also interference.

In this context, interference means any unwanted signal, noise, or disturbance that disrupts a radio signal, TV signal, phone call, Wi-Fi connection, or any other form of wireless communication.

"The phone call was full of interference because of the electrical storm."
"The old microwave was causing interference with the wireless router."
"The military used electronic interference to jam the enemy's communications."

Here, interference is always unwanted. It is the "noise" that drowns out the "signal."

In many sports, interference is the name given to a specific foul — when a player illegally gets in the way of another player or obstructs the natural flow of the game.

In American football, pass interference is called when a player illegally prevents a receiver from catching a pass — for example, by grabbing the receiver's arm or pushing them before the ball arrives.

In baseball, catcher's interference is called when the catcher's glove makes contact with the batter's bat during a swing.

In ice hockey, interference means body-checking a player who does not have the puck — you are only allowed to check the player who is carrying it.

"The referee called interference, and the team was penalized ten yards."
"It was a controversial call — the coach argued there was no interference at all."

In sports, interference always means the same thing: someone broke the rules by getting in the way.
In Law and Politics — Unlawful Obstruction or Meddling
